articles.title: WordPress Announces A Proactive Security Initiative via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
The WordPress ecosystem is experiencing a code red moment as AI lowers the barrier for criminals to identify and exploit vulnerabilities. WordPress is responding with a new security initiative that seeks to scale how it handles security to keep up with the increased number of vulnerability reports made possible by AI.

The new security initiative, called the The WordPress Core Security Initiative, is meant to improve the security of the WordPress core itself, the software that powers WordPress installations around the world. The initiative is run by the WordPress core security team and will be powered by contributions from longtime WordPress core contributors, sponsored contributors, and additional team members and volunteers.

“This work is supported by the WordPress core security team, longtime core contributors, and contributors sponsored by companies across the WordPress ecosystem.”

The announcement identifies three parts to the initiative:

Better release process This aims to make security releases faster and more reliable.

Breaking the backlog Another goal of the initiative is to clear the backlog of known security reports and issues.

Crush vulnerabilities with AI Take full advantage of AI to proactively to identify vulnerabilities faster, before researchers or attackers do.

WordPress Gets Proactive About Vulnerabilities

AI is speeding up the ability to discover vulnerabilities. WordPress has in the past relied on the ecosystem of security researchers and companies to discover vulnerabilities. The Word Security Initiative is a new approach to security that is proactive and will help to keep WordPress several steps ahead of criminals and hackers.

articles.title: What is user-generated content (UGC)? Guide for 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. User-generated content (UGC) is original content created by real customers, including reviews, photos, videos, and social posts, that brands can amplify across marketing channels.
  2. UGC builds trust faster and cheaper than traditional advertising because shoppers trust real customer experiences over branded content.
  3. A strong UGC strategy includes clear collection methods, defined content types, documented permissions, and alignment with measurable marketing goals.
  4. Hootsuite Social OS helps you manage UGC at scale: Use to track mentions and monitor hashtags and to publish and measure approved content.

What is user-generated content (UGC)?

User-generated content (UGC) is original, brand-specific content created by real customers and fans rather than by the brand itself. It can come in many forms, including videos, images, product reviews, testimonials, and even podcasts.

UGC can live everywhere: your own social channels, third-party review sites (e.g., Google and G2), community forums, blogs, or on your customers’ own social profiles.

When a happy customer posts about your product and you reshare it — like in the example below from drink brand Wildwonder — that’s UGC in action.

Source: @drinkwildwonder

In short: If a real person made it, it mentions your brand, and you didn’t produce it in-house, it counts as UGC.

Bonus !!!

Don’t know what to post on social? Unlock +100 free social media content ideas and never worry about writer’s block again!

Download now

What are the different types of user-generated content?

UGC comes in two main flavors: organic and paid. Both can show up as customer reviews, photos, videos, social media posts, or blog posts — the difference is whether money changed hands.

What is organic UGC?

Organic UGC is content your real customers share freely, without being paid or asked. It’s the most authentic type of UGC, and the kind every brand hopes to see more of.

Here are a few examples of organic UGC:

Reviews and testimonials

Online reviews are a classic form of UGC, and they work hard as social proof across your website and social channels.

Some brands even turn glowing testimonials into branded graphics to share on social. It’s an easy way to squeeze more value out of a single review.

Source: Living Proof

Photos

Photos are one of the most common types of UGC. Think: A customer showing off your product in the wild, or sharing their results after using it.

Use a niche or branded hashtag to make these posts easier to find (and reshare) later.

For example, footwear brand Asics uses the hashtag #soundmindsoundbody to collect photos from fans around the world. One quick search pulls up thousands of posts they can tap into for both content and community-building.

Source: Asics

Videos

Social videos and YouTube content are UGC gold. YouTubers regularly post “product hauls” or unboxing videos featuring multiple brands in one video. If yours gets a mention, grab that clip (with permission) and feature it on your own channels.

Social media posts

Even a quick, positive mention of your brand is worth resharing. Repost it directly on X or TikTok, or take a screenshot and turn it into a graphic for Instagram and LinkedIn. Hootsuite’s engagement tools make it easy to spot these moments as they happen.

Blog posts

Bloggers may also shout your brand out, whether it’s a full review or a passing mention in a bigger roundup. Pull a quote and share it on social or your website to extend its reach.

For example, travel blogger Nikki on Her Way casually recommends Tevas as the best brand for water shoes in her long-term packing guide. It’s a quick, unprompted endorsement that Teva could easily pull into their own content marketing.

Source: Nikki on Her Way

What is paid UGC?

Paid UGC is content made by creators you hire to talk about your product. It’s a popular option for newer brands that don’t have a big customer base sharing content organically (yet).

articles.title: FTC Claims Amazon Pocketed Over $20 Billion By ‘Manipulating’ Its Ad Auctions
articles.fullContent:
SUBSCRIPTION ONLY By Lauren Johnson ADWEEK House: Advertising HQ brings the people shaping advertising, commerce, and media together for four days of unscripted conversations and after-hours connections. Meet us in Midtown, Oct. 5–8.

The Federal Trade Commission has sued Amazon over “deceptive and unfair” advertising practices.

The lawsuit, which includes 22 U.S. state attorneys general, alleges that Amazon overcharged 1.2 million advertisers using auction rules for how ads are bought and sold, receiving more than $20 billion from these practices since 2019.

“Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices,” said FTC chairman Andrew N. Ferguson in a statement. “These higher costs were largely passed on to American consumers. The FTC under President Trump won’t allow this deception to continue.”

The complaint focuses on Amazon’s ad auction, which is used to set prices on its platform.

articles.title: WPP’s Alleged Global Rebate Scheme, Told Through Three Court Cases
articles.fullContent:
SUBSCRIPTION ONLY By Christopher Cicchiello ADWEEK House: Advertising HQ brings the people shaping advertising, commerce, and media together for four days of unscripted conversations and after-hours connections. Meet us in Midtown, Oct. 5–8.

A whistleblower suing for wrongful termination, an alleged kickback scheme, and a life sentence conviction in China are all central to WPP’s mounting legal troubles.

These three separate court cases reference an alleged illegal rebate practice carried out by WPP executives for years through media buying arm GroupM (now WPP Media).

The cases have dredged up a years-old debate about agencies pocketing media rebates, and the extent to which that practice is illegal. While rebates can be lawful—and in some jurisdictions are widely acceptable—they become an illegal “kickback” when an agent keeps money without the client’s knowledge and consent, according to the Anti-Kickback Statute.

articles.title: Callaway and Good Good’s Ad Was So Bad, Even AI Audiences Sounded the Alarm
articles.fullContent:
By Nataly Kelly The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

You know the clip by now. Good Good co-founder Garrett Clark shoves fellow creator Alexis Miestowski to the ground as she reaches for his new Callaway driver. He stands over her and tells her not to touch it.

Retailers pulled Good Good merchandise, the company withdrew as title sponsor of a PGA Tour event, while Callaway pledged $1 million to organizations working to prevent violence against women in an effort to wash away the controversy.

And the entire public argument is about approval. Callaway CEO Chip Brewer says the video was produced by Good Good but signed off by Callaway, and that “that approval should have never happened.”

On Friday morning, Good Good CEO Matt Kendrick broke an 11-year Twitter silence at 3:38 a.m. to accuse Callaway of asking for the ad, approving it, then dropping his company in a “coordinated media blitz.” Asked whether he’d sue, he replied: “Not opposed.”

Both men are addressing the wrong questions. It’s not about who approved the ad; it’s how nobody and no process stopped it before it went live, when the tools to catch the warning signs cost less than the driver they’re selling.

The story is much bigger than just one terrible ad

We’ve entered a dynamic where brands and creators need each other. Brands need creators to reach communities they can’t, while creators need to monetize their audiences.

That relationship comes with risk, as brands put decades or centuries of hard-earned equity into the hands of culturally nimble third parties, and ask them to translate it for new audiences. That’s inherently risky. It’s also increasingly necessary.

Creators aren’t the problem. The problem is that the infrastructure hasn’t kept up. Brands are producing more content, across more platforms, with more partners, for more audiences. The old model of heavily researching a few major campaigns wasn’t built for hundreds of smaller decisions.

The frustrating thing about the Good Good ad is that the warning signs weren’t particularly difficult to find. We tested the ad after it was pulled, first with U.S. consumers. It performed significantly below advertising norms on appeal, likelihood to drive behavior, brand fit, relevance, believability, and attention.

More telling was the reaction underneath those scores. Nearly one-third said there was something offensive, unpleasant, or disturbing about the ad. Shock was eight times higher than our norm.

But let’s assume the Good Good and Callaway teams involved didn’t have the time, resources, or know-how to commission a traditional market research study for one piece of creator content. Fair enough. They at least could have tested the ad with AI.

So that’s what we did at Zappi. We ran the creative past 150 AI synthetic respondents trained on real consumer response data. We had answers back in just minutes. The ad received the lowest possible score (1/5) and even synthetic respondents could spot the warning signs about the content of the ad. Its recommendation, in hindsight, is almost unbearable to read: “Soften or clarify the physical moment so it reads as playful rather than awkward.”

Testing with humans allows you to feel the fire and know exactly how hot it was. But AI was a smoke detector that, if it had only been in place, would have told people to look more closely before the brand equity went down in flames.

Now, to be very clear, AI should never be the cultural arbiter deciding what’s acceptable, but when content moves faster than the infrastructure legacy brands have at their disposal, it can be an incredibly helpful early warning system that tells a human when something deserves a second look.

Who’s at fault here? Everybody involved. Who can learn from it? Marketers. Agencies. All of us.

Creator partnerships and the creator economy aren’t going away. Neither is the pressure to produce more content, faster, for increasingly fragmented audiences.

Brands need creators, and creators need brands. Both need better guardrails, frankly, to cover their own (brand) asse(t)s.

For brands, those guardrails protect hard-earned equity. For creators, they protect the livelihood and audience they’ve spent years building. The lesson isn’t to slow creator marketing down until it resembles traditional advertising. It’s to build processes capable of moving just as fast as the media they’re meant to govern. And in this not-so-new reality, what the Callaway scandal makes clear is that AI already has an important role to play, but that many brands remain behind the curve.

Nataly Kelly is the chief marketing officer of Zappi.

articles.title: Factor Serves Up a GLP-1 Meal Plan in New Serena Williams Ad Spot
articles.fullContent:
By Andrea Michelson The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

Factor, the ready-to-eat meal kit brand, is partnering with Serena Williams for its newly launched “Let’s Eat Real” campaign .

The newest ad spot, which will air throughout the US Open, plays off of Williams’ return to tennis, with the initial ad spot opening on a tense team meeting about her career. When Williams announces she has changed her mind, the ad reveals that the tennis star is just deciding which Factor meal to eat for dinner. Another shows Williams in match mode with a timer ticking down: she is facing off with her microwave as she prepares another Factor dinner.

The partnership is set to be a multi-year collaboration, featuring a rotating menu of meals selected by Williams each month. The current lineup of the Serena Williams x Factor Collection includes a combination of high-protein dishes and some options specifically designed for people taking GLP-1 drugs.

Factor’s marketing team started courting Williams in January this year and signed her in June, Factor Chief Marketing Officer Christopher Stadler told ADWEEK. Executives at Factor had their eyes on Williams for a brand partnership months before she announced her return to tennis — so when Williams shared that she would be playing in the 2026 US Open, Factor jumped on the opportunity to market around a cultural moment.

Factor teamed up with Maximum Effort, the agency co-founded by Ryan Reynolds, to accelerate the campaign to align with Williams’ announcement. They squeezed what was meant to be a months-long lead-up into just a week of ideating and planning, culminating in a half-day shoot near Williams’ home in Palm Beach.

It was the fastest campaign turnaround Factor had ever attempted, Stadler told ADWEEK: The team filmed two full advertisements, 30 still photos, and an hour of UGC in that one quick shoot.

“We moved quickly when we saw the opportunity,” Stadler told ADWEEK. “One of our core values as a brand and as a company is the power of agility, so we put that in action with this campaign.”

Even before the partnership with Williams, Factor was making a push to include more GLP-1-friendly meal options, Stadler told ADWEEK. Over the past year and a half, the Factor menu has gone from zero to 20 percent GLP-1-friendly, which typically means small portions and nutrient-dense meals.

Williams’ athletic success and celebrity status made her a top prospect for Factor’s global ambassador role, Stadler said — and the fact that she’s been open about taking a GLP-1 was just “the icing on the cake.”

Williams, 44, is also a celebrity ambassador for the telehealth platform Ro, which provides access to GLP-1 drugs. The tennis legend has been open about taking Zepbound to aid with weight loss after her second pregnancy. Since her Wimbledon appearance earlier this summer, she is the most prominent athlete to compete at the elite level that has admitted to taking GLP-1 drugs.

For Factor, Williams represents more than just an iconic athlete, Stadler said. On top of her tennis renaissance and multiple brand partnerships, she’s also a mom to two young children — so convenience is just as important as nutrition.

“I’ve always believed that taking care of yourself starts with what you put into your body, but I also know how hard it can be to make that a priority when life gets busy,” Williams said. “Factor makes it easy to have delicious, high quality food even when my schedule is crazy, and that’s something I genuinely value.”

Andrea Michelson is the healthcare marketing reporter at ADWEEK. She previously covered the coronavirus pandemic for Business Insider and was part of the New York Times Covid mapping effort in 2020.

articles.title: ChatGPT Surpasses $1 Billion in Annualized Ads Revenue
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Stenberg The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

ChatGPT, the answer engine whose launch reshaped the digital ecosystem, surpassed a key milestone on Monday. It’s now on pace to generate more than $1 billion in advertising revenue over the next 12 months, according to the company.

The achievement, referred to as an annualized run rate, is meant to reflect the forward-looking growth of a particular line of business. It does so by extrapolating its current revenue into the future, which means that ChatGPT has not yet generated over $1 billion in annual advertising revenue but is on track to do so.

The company has previously said its goal is to surpass $2.3 billion in advertising revenue in 2026 and $100 billion by 2030.

The accomplishment, while qualified, is nonetheless a symbolic victory for the OpenAI product, which has been working to grow its advertising business to move it more quickly toward profitability.

OpenAI began testing ads inside ChatGPT in February, introduced an ads manager in March, and integrated with AppsFlyer in August.

The company now sees more than 1 billion weekly active users, 20% of whom show “commercial intent,” according to Colin Fleming , who joined the artificial intelligence firm in May as its chief marketing officer.

Its aggressive advertising build-out comes as the AI lab attempts to supplement subscription revenue, with losses continuing to outpace its gains. The company made nearly $10 billion in revenue in 2025, but its operating losses hit nearly $21 billion thanks to soaring compute costs, according to leaked financial documents .

The push to widen both its ad footprint and its enterprise business comes as OpenAI works toward a public listing. Its chief financial officer Sarah Friar reportedly told investors earlier this month that enterprise revenue has now overtaken consumer revenue, with its annual run rate topping $40 billion.

The concerted effort to stand up an advertising business serves as a key point of differentiation between OpenAI and its rival, Anthropic, which is also hurtling toward a debut on the public markets in the coming months. Anthopric has vowed never to bring advertising into its ecosystem, instead focusing its commercial strategy on serving the needs of enterprise clients that buy usage-based tokens.

Brands have experimented with advertising in ChatGPT since the ads product first launched. The company has sought to make the buying process more seamless, integrating with authoritative vendors in the space, like Adobe, Criteo, and LiveRamp, to bring measurement and attribution to its offering.

Still, the company has a lot of ground to cover before it comes close to realizing its audacious advertising goals, according to Nate Elliot, principal AI analyst at eMarketer.

“OpenAI can eventually get to parity [with Google and Meta] in terms of adtech partnerships if they want,” Elliot said. “But it’ll take time—and given the company’s burn rate, impending IPO, and astoundingly aggressive ad sales targets, time seems to be the one thing they don’t have.”

Mark Stenberg is ADWEEK's senior media reporter.

articles.fullContent:
Known and beloved for its compelling short-form video content, TikTok has become a social powerhouse in Australia. According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, 39% of Australian social users turn to TikTok to keep up with trends in many areas, from finance to fashion, technology to travel. For businesses, this level of engagement represents a major marketing opportunity—but only if they know exactly how and why Australians are using the app.

The latest TikTok statistics in Australia point to an app whose role keeps shifting. What started as an entertainment feed now shapes how Australians discover products, research big decisions and connect with the brands they love. Marketers who understand that shift meet their audience where attention already lives and turn casual scrolling into real business results.

In this guide, we cover the most important TikTok statistics in Australia to help you build a smarter, data-led strategy. With these insights, you can guide your social strategy, spark TikTok campaign ideas and create content that truly resonates with Australian audiences.

Key TikTok statistics in Australia

TikTok is a major player in Australia’s social media landscape. As of late 2025, 10.9 million Australians aged 18 and over use the app, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report. These statistics show how deeply the network has embedded itself into everyday life:

  • More than 350,000 Australian businesses use TikTok, restated by the company in 2026.

  • Australian users spend an average of 1 hour 14 minutes a day in the app (August 2025), the highest daily figure of any social app in Australia, per DataReportal and We Are Social.

  • Per a Deloitte report, Australian TikTok users spend most of their time on the app watching videos, listening to audio and browsing feeds.

  • According to Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report, short-form videos (<60 seconds long) perform best on TikTok. Users are most interested in entertaining content, product discovery and influencer partnerships

With Sprout Social, you can schedule TikTok posts, track performance and spot emerging trends from the same platform you use to manage every other network.

The rise of TikTok in Australia: TikTok stats on growth in the Australian market

Although it’s been a major player in Australia’s social media landscape for years, TikTok is constantly evolving. What primarily began as an entertainment platform has transformed into a source of information, an outlet for cultural connection and a driver for social change.

  • In Q4 2024 alone, TikTok generated 186 million downloads from users globally.

  • TikTok ads reached 51.2% of Australian adults aged 18 and over at the end of 2025, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • TikTok’s ad reach grew 13.9% year-on-year in Australia, adding 1.33 million users, the fastest growth of any major Australian platform, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • Australia counted 21.0 million social media user identities in October 2025, equal to 77.7% of the population, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • According to a 2024 report from Oxford Economics, 19% of Australian users have donated to a charity or cause they saw on TikTok, and 18% have committed their time to volunteer.

TikTok Australia user and demographic statistics

TikTok appeals strongly to younger audiences; over 30% of its global audience is aged 18–24. Given that young people are Australia’s most active social shoppers, TikTok is an ideal platform for brands to connect with and sell to these users. From gender to income, here’s a more in-depth look at Australian TikTokers:

  • Around 74% of TikTok’s Australian user base is younger than 34, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • According to Statista, around 53.1% of Australians aged 18 and over use TikTok.

  • 72% of Gen Z have TikTok accounts, compared with 50% of users overall, per Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report.

  • Almost half (48%) of Australians aged 18 to 24 use TikTok to get news, per the University of Canberra’s Digital News Report 2026.

  • According to Statista, TikTok is more popular with Gen Z than other social networks.

  • TikTok’s adult advertising audience in Australia was 53.6% male and 46.4% female in late 2025, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • Further, the 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report reveals that 37% of Millennials globally have TikTok accounts.

  • A 2024 survey found that 41% of Gen Z shoppers had made purchases through social media in the past six months, followed closely by Millennials (40%).

  • Statista reports that, while Millennials favour Facebook for social shopping, Instagram and TikTok attract more Zoomers.

Australia’s social media ban for children under 16 reshapes this picture. It removes under-16s from the platform, which shifts TikTok’s Australian audience even further towards adults. Here’s what that means for your strategy.

How does Australia’s under-16 social media ban affect TikTok?

Australia’s under-16 social media ban took effect on 10 December 2025 under the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Bill 2024. It requires TikTok and nine other social media platforms to take reasonable steps to stop Australians under 16 from holding accounts, with fines of up to A$49.5 million for non-compliance, per the eSafety Commissioner.

articles.title: How to conduct a customer experience audit rooted in social intelligence
articles.fullContent:
Your customers are already telling you where their experience is falling short. The problem is, they don’t always tell you directly.

They post about it on social media, ask questions in comments, leave Google and Yelp reviews and talk about your brand in places your customer experience team may never see. Those conversations can expose frustrations, unmet needs and changing expectations that traditional feedback channels miss.

A customer experience audit gives you a structured way to evaluate those interactions across the customer journey. Building social intelligence into the process keeps the audit grounded in what customers are saying now and helps you decide what needs attention first.

In this article, we’ll break down what a customer experience audit involves, where social intelligence fits in and how to use the findings to improve the customer journey.

What is a customer experience audit?

A customer experience audit is a structured review of how people interact with your brand across the customer journey. It examines the touchpoints and feedback that shape the experience, from initial discovery through purchase and support.

Think of it like a health check for your customer experience. You’re looking at how different parts of the journey work together and where friction shows up between channels or departments.

A strong CX audit also looks beyond the channels your business owns. Social conversations and customer care interactions add context that surveys or CRM data alone may not capture, giving you a stronger foundation for what to improve.

5 steps for a modern customer experience audit that drives action

A customer experience audit works best when you approach it systematically. Here’s how to move from deciding what you want to learn to tracking whether your changes are working.

1. Set expectations for your CX audit

Before you pull data or review touchpoints, set the audit parameters. The steps below will help you establish what you’re trying to accomplish and what it will take to get there.

Involve the right stakeholders

Customer experience rarely sits with one department. Bring in people who own different parts of the journey, such as customer care, CX, social, marketing, PR and data analysts. Each group may catch gaps others miss.

Clarify everyone’s role upfront, too. Decide who will lead the audit, who will provide data or context and who needs to act on the findings.

Determine objectives and goals

Next, decide what you want to learn or improve. You might be trying to understand why customers abandon checkout after clicking through from social, improve response times on social or figure out where the brand experience feels inconsistent across channels.

Tie those objectives to specific parts of the customer journey and the outcomes that matter most. This will guide which touchpoints and metrics you review later.

Define scope

A CX audit can expand quickly across channels, customer groups and stages of the journey, so set boundaries before you begin.

Based on your objectives, decide what needs attention now based on your specific business priorities. That might mean auditing one priority audience across the full lifecycle or zeroing in on a stage where you already know there’s friction. Future audits can broaden the scope as new questions arise.

2. Map the customer journey across touch points

Customer journeys rarely follow a neat, predictable path. People move between channels and platforms as they discover brands, weigh their options and get support, making it harder to see the full experience in one place.

Mapping those touchpoints reveals how the pieces connect and where social media plays a role.

Capture the full customer lifecycle from discovery through care

Social influences customers at several key points in their relationship with your brand:

  • Product discovery: According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, around a third of consumers prefer social search for product reviews.
  • Purchase: Sprout’s State of Influencer Marketing Report found that 86% of consumers make an influencer-inspired purchase at least once a year.
  • Customer care: The Sprout Social Index™ found that 73% of social media users expect brands to respond on social within 24 hours.

Mapping your social media marketing funnel alongside the broader customer journey helps account for those interactions from discovery through ongoing social customer care.

Look beyond owned channels

Build your audit from the places customers interact with or talk about your brand. Alongside your own social posts and ads, include replies, DMs, chatbot interactions, reviews, customer posts, social shopping activity and traffic from social to your website. Widen the lens to review sites, discussion forums, influencer communities, media coverage and mentions that may never reach your profiles.

Sprout helps bring more of those touchpoints into one workflow. The Smart Inbox centralizes incoming social messages, while Reviews pulls customer feedback from sources including Google Business Profile, Yelp, Trustpilot and TripAdvisor. Sprout Social Listening bridges direct and indirect interactions, surfacing conversations about your brand and market that may not tag or mention you directly. Together, these tools give you a broader pool of customer conversations to draw from during the audit.

Connect social with the systems other teams use, too. The Sprout Social Salesforce integration enriches CRM profiles with social data, while Sprout’s Tableau BI Connector combines social with other business data for a fuller view of the journey.

3. Use social intelligence to identify pain points and gaps in customer experience

With the customer journey mapped, it’s time to diagnose what’s happening within it. Where is frustration building? What questions keep coming up? Are expectations changing faster than your experience can keep pace with?

Social intelligence helps answer those questions by illustrating how customer sentiment and conversation patterns are changing across the market.

Analyze audience sentiment

Look at how customers feel at key points in the journey. A drop in sentiment around a product launch or an increase in negative customer care messages can point to experiences worth investigating.

Social listening helps track sentiment across broader conversations, while Sprout’s Sentiment for Messages classifies incoming messages and reviews, enabling teams to identify interactions that need attention. NewsWhip by Sprout Social further adds predictive media intelligence to indicate when stories or issues are gaining traction.

Meta decides the winner using a total value score built from several inputs:

Put Trellis on the time-consuming stuff

You didn’t get into social to spend your days pulling data, cleaning reports and packaging up findings for other people to act on.

Turn performance data into an executive summary

You know the question: How did the campaign perform? 

Giving a useful answer can mean moving between numerous dashboards and spreadsheets.  The summary may take only a few minutes to read, but it took you hours to assemble.

Instead, try asking Trellis:

Back comes three creative drivers with the posts that prove each one, written with an executive audience in mind. You bring the context and judgement; Trellis gives you a better starting point.

articles.title: What social media tasks to automate vs. outsource
articles.fullContent:
Pull reports. Route approvals. Check mentions. Schedule posts. Repeat.

Social teams have no shortage of work to do. But most of their capacity is still tied up in execution. According to our 2026 Social Intelligence Report, 80% of individual contributors say they spend more than half their time on operational work instead of the insight-driven work that moves the business forward.

AI is starting to change the equation. Social media tasks that once ate up entire afternoons can increasingly be delegated to AI agents and automated workflows. The question isn’t simply what social teams can automate, but what must be automated to keep up.

This article breaks down which tasks are best handed off to AI, where human judgment still matters and how automation can give social teams more room to focus on higher-value work.

Social media manager tasks: A daily overview

A social media manager’s day covers a lot more than planning content and hitting publish. Here are some social media tasks that fall under most social media job titles:

  • Respond to comments and messages across platforms
  • Monitor brand mentions, relevant keywords and industry conversations
  • Curate and create engaging content
  • Schedule posts for the next day, week or month
  • Analyze metrics to gauge performance
  • Brainstorm content ideas
  • Research trending topics and conversations
  • Manage paid social media campaigns
  • Vet and coordinate with creators and influencers
  • Handle crisis communication, as needed

Which of these are you still doing manually? Look at each task and ask: Could AI handle it? Or does it still need a person’s judgment?

Automated tasks in social media marketing: What AI can do now

A few years ago, most social media tasks required a person at every step. Now, AI handles a growing share of the daily workload, from scheduling to reporting to the first pass on customer replies.

Here’s where it’s already doing the heavy lifting.

Publishing & scheduling

Getting a post approved and published can often involve a few rounds of email or Slack follow-ups with your manager or other stakeholders. Automated approval workflows remove that back-and-forth by sending content directly to the right person at the right stage.

Choosing when to post has also become more precise. Instead of relying on generic best-practice windows, AI can analyze when your specific audience is most likely to engage. Sprout’s Optimal Send Times with ViralPost uses your audience’s behavior to recommend the best publishing times.

Alt text is another task that can slip when deadlines get tight. AI can help by generating descriptive alt text within the publishing workflow, making accessibility easier to build into the process. Sprout’s Generate ALT Text capability does this directly in the platform.

Reporting & insights

Building a report for leadership can mean pulling data from multiple dashboards, organizing it into a deck and then explaining what changed and why. AI can cut down that work by letting teams query social data in plain language instead of rebuilding the analysis from scratch each time. With Sprout’s Trellis, social teams, leaders and cross-functional partners can ask questions about social performance and get answers without waiting for someone to pull a report.

That also makes social data more accessible and useful outside the social team. If someone in product or customer care wants to know how a launch went or understand customer sentiment, they can get the answer directly by asking an AI agent.

Social listening & media intelligence

Thousands of conversations can unfold around your brand, competitors and industry in a matter of hours. AI helps teams sort through that volume by analyzing conversations for patterns, shifts in sentiment and emerging topics that would be difficult to catch manually.

Within Sprout Listening, Trellis takes that a step further by letting teams ask questions about sentiment, share of voice or emerging themes in plain language and get answers based on their listening data.

AI can also help teams spot reputation risks earlier. NewsWhip by Sprout Social analyzes real-time signals across social and the web to predict which stories are likely to gain traction. Teams get an earlier read on what’s picking up steam and more time to decide how to respond.

Influencer/creator discovery & vetting

Finding the right creators can take hours of scrolling profiles and comparing audiences to see if someone is a good fit for the brand. AI speeds up that research by narrowing a large pool of creators to a smaller set based on specific criteria.

Sprout Social Influencer Marketing’s natural-language search lets teams describe the type of creator they’re looking for and returns relevant matches, along with brand-fit scoring and brand safety checks. Creator managers can spend less time on manual research and more time reviewing the strongest options, reaching out and building relationships.

Social customer care

Customer messages don’t stop at the end of the day, and some need attention faster than others. AI can help care teams triage incoming comments and DMs by analyzing sentiment and identifying messages that may need a quicker response.

Sprout’s Smart Inbox brings messages from across networks into one place and helps teams prioritize what to address first. It can also draft responses for customer care agents to review and personalize, accelerating personalization while cutting down the time spent writing routine replies from scratch.

Social media management tasks that still need a human

AI can pull data, spot patterns and draft a response. But it can’t navigate internal politics, interpret culture, earn trust or persuade a leader to invest more in social.

Automating routine work gives social teams more time for the parts of the job that depend on judgment, context and relationships.

Cross-functional relationships & influencing up

Getting another team to act on social insights takes more than sending them a report. Social leaders need to understand what product, customer care or sales is trying to solve, then connect social data to the decisions already on their plate.

Leadership buy-in works the same way. A strong business case can support a request for more budget or headcount, but the numbers rarely do all the work. Leaders are more likely to invest when they trust the person making the recommendation and understand how it connects to broader priorities.

articles.title: The Practical Guide to Google Analytics 4
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Google renamed “Conversions” to “Key Events” in 2024. The terms mean different things in GA4 and Google Ads, so getting the terminology right matters when comparing numbers across platforms. 
  • Every interaction in GA4 is event-based, with parameters providing the context behind what happened.
  • Data-driven attribution is GA4’s default model, using machine learning to spread credit across all the touchpoints that led to a conversion. 
  • BigQuery export is free for standard properties and unlocks analysis that the standard reports can’t handle. 
  • DebugView is the fastest way to catch broken tracking before it becomes weeks of unusable data.

Are you getting the most out of Google Analytics 4 (GA4)?

GA4 has been Google’s standard analytics platform for a few years now. The move from Universal Analytics (UA) was a major shift, but Google has continued updating GA4 itself along the way. One of the biggest changes came in 2024, when Google replaced “Conversions” with “Key Events” in 2024. 

While some marketers might miss UA, there’s no going back.

This GA4 guide skips the history lesson and focuses on what you need to do in GA4 day to day, from proper setup to tracking key events (not conversions) and other impactful metrics.

What Is Google Analytics 4?

Google Analytics 4 is the current version of Google Analytics, and it provides web analytics on a level that allows marketers to effectively analyze important customer usage metrics, not just track traffic.

Before we get into the details, here’s a quick Google Analytics 4 overview. 

Google Analytics 4 tracks the entire customer path across multiple platforms and leverages AI and machine learning to provide more detailed insights into how users interact with your website and app.

GA4 combines cross-channel measurement and AI-driven predictive analytics. It also operates under a privacy-first tracking framework designed for today’s privacy laws, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). 

These features combine to give marketers a more complete view of how users interact with their digital properties than what UA offered.

How to Set Up Google Analytics 4

Many marketers ask me how to use GA4. Your setup process will depend on whether you’re tracking a website or an app (or both). I’ve broken down each option below.

Google Analytics for Firebase

Firebase is Google’s app development platform that helps you build and deploy apps and games. If you enable Google Analytics when creating a Firebase project, Firebase automatically links your app to a GA4 property.  

If you’re working with an older Firebase project, you may need to link it to a GA4 property or complete Google’s upgrade process.

To upgrade your Firebase account to Google Analytics 4, follow these steps:

  1. Log in to the Firebase console.
  2. Go to Analytics > Dashboard on the left panel.
  3. Follow any prompts to enable or upgrade GA for the project. 

Once linked, you can find app analytics in both the Firebase console and Google Analytics.

Setting up Google Analytics 4 from Scratch

If you’ve never used Google Analytics before or you want to set up a brand-new website, you’ll need to start from scratch:

  • Create an Analytics account if you haven’t already by visiting https://analytics.google.com and opening Admin. Then click Create, and then Account (skip if you already have an account).
  • In the Property column, click Create > Property.
  • Enter a name for your new property, and select a time zone and currency. 
  • Select your industry category and business size.
  • Select your business objectives (e.g., “Get baseline reports,” “Generate leads”).
  • Click Create and accept the Terms of Service.
  • Add a data stream (Web, iOS, or Android) to start collecting data.

Source: https://www.eridesignstudio.com/insights/set-up-a-google-analytics-4-property/

A data stream is a source of information that feeds your GA4 analytics property. It could be your website or your app. Google will guide you through adding each data stream.

Install With Google Tag Manager

For most marketers, Google Tag Manager (GTM) is the recommended installation method. GTM lets you deploy and update the GA4 tag (along with other marketing tags) without touching the site code whenever something changes.

To set up, create a free GTM account and add a container for your site. Google will give you two snippets of code to paste on every page (one in the <head>, one right after the opening <body> tag). 

Once the container is live, create a Google tag inside GTM using your GA4 Measurement ID and set it to fire on all pages. Publish the container to push your changes live.

Verify With DebugView

After setup, use DebugView (found under Admin) to confirm your events are firing correctly. It shows real-time event data from a single device with debug mode enabled, which beats waiting for reports to populate. Skipping this step is a common way for broken tracking to go unnoticed for weeks.

articles.title: The best competitive intelligence software in 2026
articles.fullContent:
If your competitive research involves jumping between LinkedIn, G2, and an overgrown collection of bookmarked pricing pages, there’s a better way.

Competitive intelligence software automates the detective work, surfacing the competitor moves that actually matter. 

Let’s take a closer look at the best platforms for tracking competitors across sales, search, social, and beyond.

Key takeaways

  1. Best tools at a glance: Crayon and Contify for all-in-one platforms, Lumen and Brand24 for social and brand intelligence, Klue and Clozd for sales enablement, and Similarweb and Semrush for digital intelligence.
  2. There’s no one-size-fits-all tool. The right pick depends on whether you’re tracking deals, website traffic, or brand chatter.
  3. Test it inside your real workflow. If a tool requires constant cleanup or five new steps, it’s not worth it.

What is competitive intelligence software?

Competitive intelligence software is a tool that helps companies monitor competitors and turn external information into business insights.

For example, marketing teams might use it to see which keywords a rival is ranking for, while product development teams might use it to catch new features early.

You could do all of this manually, but that means refreshing competitor websites, pricing pages, and review sites on repeat. These tools bring those signals into one place, so you can spend more time deciding your next steps.

Bonus !!!

Get a free, customizable competitive analysis template to easily size up the competition and identify opportunities for your brand to pull ahead.

Download now

What kinds of competitor data does it track?

Most competitive intelligence tools monitor some mix of the following:

  • Pricing changes: A new tier, a sudden discount, or a reshuffled package can tell you a lot about who a competitor is trying to win over.
  • Product launches and messaging shifts: Catch new features, positioning pivots, and changes in how competitors talk about their value.
  • Web traffic and SEO performance: Track which keywords competitors are winning, where their traffic comes from, and which parts of their site are pulling the most weight.
  • Social share of voice and sentiment: Find out who’s dominating the conversation online (and whether that conversation is positive, negative, or somewhere in between).
  • Reviews and community chatter: Buyers are pretty honest on sites like G2 and Reddit. That candor is gold when you’re sizing up the competition.
  • Hiring activity: Job postings can be surprisingly revealing. A sudden hiring spree in AI, enterprise sales, or a new region can hint at what’s coming next.
  • Company news and funding: Leadership changes, acquisitions, earnings transcripts, and funding rounds often signal big moves before they show up in the product.

No single tool tracks all of this equally well, which is why the best pick depends on what your team actually needs to watch. More on that next.

What are the main types of competitive intelligence software?

Competitive intelligence software falls into four main types: all-in-one platforms, sales enablement tools, digital market intelligence tools, and social and brand intelligence tools. Here’s how they compare:

All-in-one competitive intelligence platforms

These platforms try to cover the whole competitive picture. They pull together signals like competitor news and product updates, then package them into competitor profiles, alerts, and digests for your team.

These tools are a good fit when:

  • You want one central home for competitive intel
  • Multiple teams (sales, product, marketing) all need access to the same insights
  • You’d rather get a weekly digest than dig for updates yourself

But, the trade-off: All-in-one tools cover a lot of ground, but specialized tools usually dig deeper in their specific lane.

Sales enablement platforms

Sales enablement tools are built for the moment a competitor comes up in a deal. They arm reps with battlecards, win/loss insights, and objection-handling answers. They typically integrate with CRMs like Salesforce.

Digital market intelligence

These tools track how competitors perform online, which makes them a favorite for marketing and growth teams.

Most cover:

  • Traffic estimates: How much traffic competitors get and which channels drive it

articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media monitoring is the practice of tracking brand mentions, keywords, and conversations across social platforms to understand what people are saying about your brand, your competitors, and your industry.
  2. Monitoring helps teams catch reputation risks early, respond to customers faster, and surface insights that inform marketing, product, and sales decisions.
  3. AI-powered monitoring tools can now analyze sentiment, detect crises, and surface trends across millions of sources in real time.
  4. The best monitoring strategies share insights across the organization, not just the social team, and measure ROI tied to business outcomes.

What is social media monitoring?

Social media monitoring is the process of tracking what people are saying about your brand on social media.

This includes both tagged and untagged mentions, whether they show up in comments on your own accounts or in conversations happening elsewhere across the social web.

In practice, that scope is wider than most teams expect. Monitoring covers posts, comments, replies, reviews, video captions, forum threads, and news coverage across networks like Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, and Bluesky, where 84% of U.S. adults use YouTube and 71% use Facebook. Most of those conversations never tag your handle, which is exactly why manual checking falls short.

How does social media monitoring work?

Social media monitoring isn’t just one activity. It’s a mix of signals that, together, tell you what people are saying about your brand, your competitors, and your industry.

Here are the key components that make up social media monitoring:

  • Brand mentions: Track when people talk about your brand across comments, posts, and conversations. This is your baseline signal, and it covers both direct tags and untagged references.
  • Sentiment analysis: Understand how people feel about your brand by looking at whether mentions are positive, negative, or neutral. Tracked over time, sentiment tells you whether perception is improving or slipping.
  • Competitor analysis: Keep tabs on what people are saying about your competitors, including their campaigns, products, and gaps. Their weak spots are often your opportunities.
  • Industry trends: Follow larger conversations in your industry, including trending topics, hashtags, and viral moments, so you can join them while they still matter.
  • Influencer identification: Find people already talking about your brand who could become partners or advocates. Existing fans usually convert into partnerships faster than cold outreach.
  • Share of voice (SOV): Measure how much of the conversation your brand owns compared to competitors. It’s one of the clearest ways to benchmark visibility.
  • Crisis detection: Catch spikes in mentions or shifts in sentiment early, so you can respond before things escalate.
  • Hashtag tracking: Monitor how your branded hashtags, campaign tags, and industry keywords are performing.
  • AI-powered analysis: Use AI to cluster themes, flag anomalies, and summarize what thousands of mentions add up to, instead of reading them one by one.

Together, these signals turn everyday social conversations into actionable insights for your team.

Social media monitoring vs. social listening: what’s the difference?

The short answer: monitoring tracks individual conversations as they happen, and social listening analyzes those conversations in aggregate to find patterns. They’re closely related, but they serve different purposes.

  • Social monitoring is reactive. It focuses on tracking mentions and responding to what’s happening in real time.
  • Social listening is proactive. It starts by analyzing the information from social monitoring to spot larger patterns and trends. In other words, it looks at the bigger picture to improve your social media marketing strategy over time.

For example, social media monitoring identifies comments about your brand online that could use an immediate response from your social or customer service teams.

Source: Warby Parker

Social media listening takes a step back and looks at those same comments over time to see how sentiment is changing.

What is a social media SWOT analysis?

A social media SWOT analysis is a framework marketers use to evaluate their social media performance by looking at four areas: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.

  • Deciding whether to join a new social media platform
  • Rebranding or repositioning

As the hub of cultural conversations and online activity, social media provides valuable intelligence to inform business strategies. It’s how you discover everything from what trends are taking over to what products people are buying. In fact, the 2026 Social Intelligence Report found that half of one-person teams consider it mission-critical for future growth.

But between crafting content and staying on top of communications, managing social media is hard enough when you’re the only one on the team. This leaves you with little time to focus on social intelligence, let alone extract insights to fuel business growth.

In this post, we provide a guideline on how to streamline social media management for one-person teams. From strategic automation to structured task management, we show you how you can save time and focus on more high-impact work. Let’s get started.

What it means to run social alone

When you’re running social media on your own, you’re juggling multiple roles. You’re the one coming up with content ideas and bringing those ideas to fruition by writing captions and designing graphics. At the same time, you’re in charge of publishing the content, managing comments, responding to DMs and analyzing your data.

You’re essentially doing everything by yourself all at once.

As it is, social media marketers are already at risk of burning out and running out of content ideas. The 2025 Sprout Social Index TM notes that 33% of marketers fear burnout and creative fatigue.

The risk gets significantly bigger for someone who’s constantly overwhelmed because they’re doing it all alone. Yet this is what social media management looks like for most startups and small business operations.

The biggest challenges for a one-person team

To start with, you need to pinpoint what actually makes it challenging to manage social media on your own. That way, you can focus your efforts on tackling those specific challenges. Let’s dig deeper into the biggest problems in social media management for one-person teams.

Constant context-switching across platforms

One minute you’re checking your Facebook stats, the next you’re trying to catch up on all your Instagram DMs and messages. When you’re a one-person social media team, you’re constantly switching between different tasks across platforms. So you’re distracted and unable to focus on a single task, which will affect productivity.

It’s even worse when you’re doing everything manually. According to The Social Media Productivity Report, 63% of social media marketers report not being able to do high-impact work because of manual tasks.

Creative and content fatigue

Social media teams have to always be on top of trending memes and viral topics to keep producing relevant content. According to the 2025 Sprout Social Index TM , 94% of social media practitioners report having to be chronically online to do their jobs.

Ultimately, the social media burnout catches up, especially when you’re the only one coming up with ideas and producing content. That’s why burnout and creative fatigue rank as the fourth greatest fear among social media marketers.

Proving ROI without a dedicated analyst

When you’re the only one on your team, you’re also in charge of collecting performance data and putting together reports. It’s easy enough to point out which content is performing well or how your page has grown over time. But without a dedicated analyst to interpret your data, you’ll have a hard time aligning your social media investment to actual business outcomes.

Keeping up with response-time expectations

Between the content creation and performance analysis, comments and DMs often go unanswered for hours when you’re a one-person team. This could reflect poorly on the customer experience, especially with consumers expecting swift responses on social media.

As the 2025 Sprout Social Index TM found, almost three-quarters of consumers expect brands to respond within 24 hours. They’ll even buy from a competitor next time if the brand doesn’t respond to their customer service questions on social.

3 tips for prioritizing when everything feels urgent

You’re a few days behind on content and your DMs are flooded with messages that you haven’t been able to check. For one-person social teams, it seems like there’s a never-ending to-do list where every item needs to be done “right now.” Here’s how you can streamline your tasks and figure out what to prioritize:

1. Set 2–3 goals tied to business outcomes, not vanity metrics

Impressions are great, but what do they actually mean for your business? Have a clear idea of what you want to get out of social media. This will serve as the foundation for the rest of your social media marketing strategy, shaping everything from your content to your analytics.

Start with 2-3 goals that are related to actual business outcomes. For instance:

  • Growing brand awareness
  • Building a brand community
  • Improving brand sentiment
  • Generating online sales
  • Driving qualified leads
  • Preventing customer churn
  • Speeding up social customer service

2. Use an impact-vs-effort framework to triage daily tasks

Building a framework for prioritizing tasks will help you organize your schedule more strategically. Weigh the expected value of each task against the effort needed to complete it, so you can sort out the order in which to do them.

For example:

Quick wins (high impact, low effort)

  • What they are: Tasks that yield high value and require very little time or money
  • Examples: Repurposing existing content into graphics and bite-sized social posts, sharing user-generated content, customizing social media templates for new ideas, actively replying to recent comments

Big bets (high impact, high effort)

  • What they are: Tasks that yield high value and require heavy planning, time and/or budget
  • Examples: Running an influencer marketing campaign, launching a multi-platform content series

Backups (low impact, low effort)

  • What they are: Minor tasks that don’t add significant value but take very little time to complete
  • Examples: Making small tweaks to your profile, engaging with content from other brands/creators

Time sinkers (low impact, high effort)

  • What they are: Time-consuming tasks that yield little to no return on investment
  • Examples: Manually tracking and analyzing vanity metrics, designing complex custom graphics for platforms that your audience doesn’t use

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Franchise costs range widely. A home-based franchise starts at around $10,000, while a McDonald’s franchise ranges from $1.47 million to $2.73 million per its 2026 FDD. 
  • Every franchisor must provide a Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD). Use it to compare key factors such as fee structures and available support and financing across brands. 
  • Marketing is critical from day one. Brand awareness gets customers searching, but the franchise location with the strongest local marketing presence wins. 
  • Local SEO and geo-targeted paid ads are the two highest-ROI channels for new franchisees, closely followed by social media that stays within brand guidelines. 
  • Franchise earnings vary widely. Franchisees in the food and beverage space can earn anywhere from under $50,000 to over $250,000.

Learning how to start a franchise can be a great way to become a business owner. To launch a business, you need to perform market research, file for a license, create a marketing plan, and build your brand. Buying a franchise location within a corporation that’s already taken all those steps is one way to shorten that learning curve.

Becoming a franchise business owner also enables you to tap into a large brand’s resources and branding, but that doesn’t mean you should leave the marketing completely up to them.

Savvy entrepreneurs who start a franchise business understand the importance of taking all the right steps from start to finish. That’s exactly what I’m here to show you in this guide.

We’ll cover the basics, like how to start a franchise and the initial costs. Then we’ll move on to the engine that makes your franchise a success: learning how to market it once it’s open.

How Does a Franchise Business Work?

In a franchise business, a franchise owner pays a fee to essentially “rent” a brand name. The franchisee runs the business themselves (or hires someone to do so) and must follow the rules and regulations governing brand use.

For example, many McDonald’s restaurants are franchises, meaning an owner (or group of owners, in some cases) pays McDonald’s to use their brand name, menus, logos, and other business assets.

They run their location, pay McDonald’s to use the name, and keep the remaining profits.

A franchise business is a popular business model because it offers owners the best of both worlds: the support of a large brand and the benefits of owning a business.

Key Takeaways

  • Paid media forecasts most often break at CPC inflation and conversion rate volatility, not at the strategy level.
  • New campaigns run negative for the first several weeks as algorithms learn. Forecasts that skip this ramp-up period set expectations that fail before the campaign does.
  • Creative decay is a predictable variable that belongs in every paid forecast from day one.
  • AI bidding on Google and Meta is reducing predictability. Bid strategy adjustments have less direct impact than most teams assume.
  • The paid forecasting framework runs in sequence: forecast reach, then efficiency, then profitability. Each step feeds the next.

Your forecast said this campaign would hit a 4x ROAS by month two. Instead, CPCs are up, CTR is sliding, and leadership is asking questions you don’t have good answers to.

This isn’t a strategy problem. It’s a forecasting problem.

Most paid media forecasts fail not because marketers are bad at math, but because they rely on assumptions that don’t survive contact with real auction behavior. CPC inflation, conversion rate volatility, creative decay, and AI bidding unpredictability all create gaps between what the model projected and what the campaign actually delivered.

This post covers what causes those gaps and how to build paid media forecasting models that account for real-world variables from the start, so your next forecast holds up.

Why Paid Media Forecasts Miss

Most paid forecasts break at the same pressure points. Identifying which variable caused a miss is as important as building the next forecast, because the same failure tends to repeat if you don’t isolate the cause.

Source

CPC inflation. CPCs are driven by auction dynamics, not advertiser intention. Competitive pressure, quality score changes, and platform algorithm updates can push CPCs above forecast assumptions faster than most models account for. NP Digital data from campaigns across industries shows CPC inflation leads paid forecast failures at 54 percent, making it the single most common cause of forecast drift.

Conversion rate volatility. Conversion rates don’t hold steady across changing conditions. They compress when buyer confidence drops and expand during periods of strong demand, regardless of traffic quality. A constant conversion rate assumption during an economic downturn is actually a win. A constant assumption during a category boom is a miss waiting to happen. Volatility in conversion rates is always relative to what’s happening outside the platform.

Creative decay. As creative fatigue sets in across any audience, CTR drops and effective CPCs rise. If the forecast doesn’t account for a creative refresh cadence, the model drifts optimistic over the life of the campaign. Creative decay is not an edge case. It is a predictable curve.

AI bidding unpredictability. Automated bidding systems on Google Ads and Meta optimize toward signals the advertiser does not fully control. Teams often assume they can compensate for a weak period by adjusting bids. In practice, bid strategy changes have less direct impact than most assume, because the algorithm is making more of the decisions.

Audience overlap across platforms. When the same audience is targeted across multiple channels simultaneously, reach projections overstate real incremental reach and efficiency metrics overstate actual performance. A lead attributed to paid search and a lead attributed to paid social may be the same person, and the forecast rarely accounts for that.

The Ramp-Up Curve: Why New Campaigns Run Negative First

Forecasting average performance from day one is one of the most reliable ways to lose leadership trust in a new campaign. New paid campaigns almost always run negative through the first several weeks, and a forecast that doesn’t show this sets expectations the campaign will fail to meet before it finds its footing.

The reason is structural. New campaigns require time for bid algorithms to gather enough conversion signals to optimize effectively, for audience targeting to sharpen based on early engagement data, and for creative performance data to inform delivery decisions. During this learning phase, CPCs are typically higher than steady state and conversion rates are lower. That combination produces a negative return that looks like failure but is actually normal.

This effect is most pronounced in Performance Max and Advantage+ campaigns, where the algorithm has broader targeting latitude and less historical data to draw on at launch. Campaigns built on new creative, new landing pages, or new audiences extend the ramp-up period further.

The practical implication for ad forecasting is to model week-by-week profitability, not campaign-average profitability. A campaign that looks marginally profitable in aggregate may be deeply negative in weeks one through three and significantly profitable from week six onward. A flat average across the campaign period hides the early risk and the later opportunity, and gives leadership no framework for interpreting early results.

Teams that show leadership the ramp-up curve before it happens get the time to let campaigns mature. Teams that don’t tend to get pulled before the algorithm has learned anything useful.

The Three-Step Paid Forecasting Framework

A reliable forecast marketing campaign model answers questions in sequence: how many people will see your ads, how many will act on them, and what will the business get in return. articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. The 10 types of social media interactions are comments, shares, saves, direct messages, tags and mentions, likes and reactions, follows and unfollows, reviews and ratings, social search actions, and interactive content like polls and quizzes.
  2. Not all interactions carry equal weight. Comments, shares, saves, and DMs signal stronger intent than likes alone and have a bigger impact on reach and conversions.
  3. Measuring interaction quality, not just volume, helps teams prove social’s business impact and refine their strategy.
  4. A connected social operating system like Hootsuite Social OS helps teams track, respond to, and learn from interactions across every platform in one place.

What is social media interaction?

Social media interaction is any exchange between a brand and a user on a social platform. That includes likes, comments, direct messages, tags, saves, shares, reviews, and follows.

Interactions happen everywhere 5.75 billion people spend time on social, not just in the feed. They show up in stories, in comment threads, in the DM inbox, and increasingly in search results inside apps like TikTok and Instagram.

The key thing to remember is that interaction is two-way communication. A user can start it, or your brand can. Both directions count, and both shape how people see you.

Get a free step-by-step social media strategy guide   with pro tips on how to grow your social media presence.

Download now

What is the difference between social media interaction and engagement?

A social media interaction is a single action someone takes, while engagement is the broader measure of how actively your audience interacts with your content over time. In other words, interactions are the individual moments, and engagement is the pattern those moments create.

Why are social media interactions important?

Social media interactions are how people connect with your brand, and vice versa. Every interaction is a chance to build a relationship, answer a question, or move someone closer to a purchase.

There are three reasons interactions deserve attention beyond the vanity metric:

  • They build brand loyalty and trust: Replying to a comment or resolving a DM turns a passive follower into someone with a reason to come back.
  • They influence social search and discovery: Comments, saves, and shares feed the ranking signals platforms use to surface content in feeds and in-app search results.
  • They support customer service and community: A growing share of support questions now arrive as comments and DMs rather than emails or phone calls.

Square’s research on the future of commerce found that interacting with brands is a key part of the buying journey. For example, 46% of consumers want to communicate with businesses through social media platforms.

Summary: Social media interactions open the door to deeper engagement, stronger relationships, and ultimately, conversions.

How consumers expect to interact with brands in 2026

Expectations have shifted in three ways worth planning around.

First, private channels are doing more work. Social users spend more time in DMs, and more sales and support conversations now start in the inbox, which makes the DM thread a customer service channel, not just a marketing one.

Second, people expect speed. A question left sitting for days reads as a non-answer, and it is often visible to everyone else scrolling your comments.

Third, people want interactions that sound human. A reply written like a press release lands worse than a short, direct one.

10 types of social media interactions and how to respond

Here are the 10 most common types of social media interactions, roughly ordered from highest to lowest intent:

  1. Comments and conversations
  2. Shares
  3. Saves
  4. Direct messages
  5. Tags and mentions
  6. Likes and reactions
  7. Follows and unfollows
  8. Reviews and ratings
  9. Social search clicks and actions
  10. Polls, quizzes, and interactive content

1. Comments and conversations

Comments are when users reply directly to your posts, whether that’s with text, emojis, or by tagging other accounts. They’re also the interaction most likely to turn into a real conversation.

Think of comments as soft leads. Someone stopped scrolling, paid attention to your content, and took the time to respond. That’s intent.

Comment threads also carry weight in algorithm prioritization. When a post keeps generating replies, platforms read that as a signal the content is worth showing to more people. Your own replies count toward that activity.

But if you’re ghosting your own comment section, you’re missing out on opportunities to move potential customers closer to decision. That’s why responding back matters.

Key Takeaways

  • SEO forecasting still matters, but the inputs and outputs have changed. 
  • AI Overviews and zero-click behavior are absorbing demand that used to produce clicks. Forecasts built on pre-AI assumptions will now overstate expected traffic.
  • The modern forecasting model is probabilistic and scenario-based, not linear. Express outputs as ranges across conservative, expected, and aggressive cases.
  • Influence metrics are the bridge that translate SEO visibility into business value. Examples of influence metrics include branded search demand growth, CTR behavior and conversion rates.

When it comes to SEO, forecasting can be a tricky concept.

You’re trying to predict the future of your website’s traffic and it can be difficult to know which metrics to focus on. It can also be difficult to know if the metrics you selected are giving you and your team a clear picture.

That picture has gotten harder to read. AI Overviews, zero-click behavior, and LLM-referred traffic have changed what SEO forecasts need to measure and how the results need to be presented. 

This is why many SEO forecasts are starting to break down. Rankings may improve while clicks flatten. Traffic may increase without revenue following. And visibility may influence demand long before a user ever lands on your site. Modern SEO forecasting needs to explain that disconnect, not hide it.

In this article, we’ll discuss what SEO forecasting is, and where it is and isn’t effective. We’ll also look at the different types of forecasting you can use, as well as the pros and cons of each method. Finally, we’ll cover some of the overall limitations of SEO forecasting as a concept, and what you may want to consider instead.

Let’s start by discussing the potential value of SEO forecasting in the first place.

What Is SEO Forecasting and Why Does It Matter?

SEO forecasting is the practice of predicting and estimating changes in your website’s search engine visibility. This includes factors such as organic traffic, keyword rankings, and more. By trying to predict the future, you can plan ahead and make educated decisions about how to best optimize your website for search engine results pages (SERPs).

For example, let’s say you noticed that your website is losing traffic due to changes in the SERPs. In this case, you may try to use SEO forecasting to help you identify potential issues and strategize how to improve your website’s visibility.

Knowing where your website stands in terms of SEO today is important, but understanding where it’s going in the future is even more critical. With SEO forecasting, in theory, you can identify potential problems and take action to address them before they become a reality. This could include creating content around specific topics or introducing new strategies like link building.

Source: Simplilearn

When used in the right context, SEO forecasting can help give you an idea of performance over time, so you can track progress and adjust as needed. It may also help you stay ahead of the competition and ensure your website is always optimized for success.

With that said, whenever someone asks my NP Digital team about forecasting, we always try to provide a clear picture of what forecasting can and can’t do.

An SEO forecast isn’t going to magically predict the entire future landscape for you. There are too many factors to consider, from seasonality to greater economic trends, that can affect your organic growth and won’t get tracked in any forecast.

So when we talk about SEO forecasting and its benefits, they are best served to help you make decisions, not be your sole source of truth. In addition, if you decide to use them, that needs to be done alongside general best practices like experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness (E-E-A-T), as well as your previous successes or struggles.

Remember, you can’t truly pinpoint search performance until after the fact, which applies to just about any marketing context, really.

The search landscape has also changed materially since most forecasting frameworks were built. AI Overviews, zero-click behavior, and LLM-referred traffic all affect how rankings translate to traffic and how traffic translates to revenue. A forecast that doesn’t account for these shifts will consistently overstate expected results.

Why Most SEO Forecasts Are Breaking Down Now

Most SEO forecasting models were built on assumptions that are no longer relevant. Sessions are often treated as equivalent to conversions. In practice, traffic and conversions have decoupled. AI Overviews are answering queries without producing clicks, which means impression counts can rise while visit counts fall. A model that treats session volume as a reliable conversion proxy will overstate business outcomes.

Conversion rates are often held constant, yet they shift with buyer intent, market conditions, and the competitive landscape. A model that holds conversion rate constant across changing conditions will produce projections that drift from reality the longer the forecast runs.

A growing share of searches now end without a click to any website, especially informational and navigational queries where AI-generated answers absorb demand before users reach organic listings. Lumping all query types together in a forecast produces misleading averages, because transactional and commercial queries retain click volume at higher rates.

How Query Fanouts Actually Work

When a user asks ChatGPT a question, the model does not simply search for that exact phrase. It executes a set of related sub-queries behind the scenes, each exploring a different angle of the original prompt, then merges those results to build its response. That set of sub-queries is the fanout.

A question like “best project management tools for remote teams” might produce fanouts for “top project management software 2026,” “remote team collaboration features,” “project management pricing comparison,” and “enterprise versus small team project management tools,” all running simultaneously. The answer ChatGPT provides draws from all of those sources combined, not just from content that matches the original wording.
